questions.q: What does telnet <host> 1433 test that ping alone does not?
options: Whether something is actually listening and accepting TCP connections on the SQL Server port
Whether SQL Server Agent is running
Whether the SQL Server login credentials are valid
Whether the remote database exists
questions.explain: Ping only confirms basic network reachability; telnet to the specific port tests whether a service is actually listening and accepting connections there.

questions.q: Why does a named instance typically require SQL Server Browser for client connections?
options: Browser is required for every SQL Server connection, named or default
Named instances cannot use TCP/IP at all
Named instances always use port 1433, same as default instances
A named instance usually listens on a dynamically assigned port, and Browser resolves the instance name to that actual port
questions.explain: Browser (UDP 1434) resolves an instance name like SQLSRV02\PROD to the dynamic port that instance is actually listening on.

questions.q: A client can't connect to a named instance, but the instance itself is healthy and TCP/IP is enabled. What's a classic cause per this lesson?
options: The client is using an outdated version of SSMS
The SQL Server Browser service is stopped
The database is in single-user mode
The SQL Server error log has been deleted
questions.explain: If Browser isn't running, a client that doesn't already know the exact dynamic port can fail to connect even though the named instance itself is completely healthy.

questions.q: What symptom does a blocked firewall rule produce, compared to a stopped SQL Server service?
options: A firewall block always produces a clear 'firewall blocked' error message to the client
A firewall block only affects local connections, never remote ones
The exact same symptom — a connection that fails before authentication is ever attempted
A firewall block causes a login failure, not a connection failure
questions.explain: Both a blocked firewall and a stopped service prevent the connection before SQL Server authentication logic ever runs, making them indistinguishable from the client's point of view without further checks.

questions.q: If the network path (ping/telnet) is confirmed open but the connection still fails, where should you look next?
options: The client machine's installed fonts
The SQL Server error log, for login failures or connection-refused entries
The Windows Event Viewer's Application log only, never SQL Server's own log
The DNS server logs exclusively
questions.explain: Once the network layer is confirmed open, the SQL Server error log is the next place to check — it records login failures and server-side connection rejections around the time of the attempt.
